Salzburg
SALTS-boorg
n. (the Austrian archbishopric whose archbishop expelled some twenty thousand Protestants in 1731 and 1732, many of whom settled in Georgia)
From Old High German salz, salt, and burg, a fortress, for the salt trade of the Salzach.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Salzburg was a Roman town, a see from 739 under Rupert and Virgil, and from the fourteenth century an independent archbishopric whose prince-archbishops ruled a mountain state until 1803. Protestantism survived in its Alpine valleys, especially the Defereggen and the Pongau, among miners and farmers who kept Lutheran books for two centuries. In 1731 Archbishop Leopold Anton von Firmian issued an edict of emigration; in the winter of 1731 and the spring of 1732 some twenty thousand people were expelled, many given only days to leave and forced to sell their holdings at a loss, and children under twelve were retained to be raised Catholic. Frederick William the First of Prussia settled most of them in East Prussia; one party reached the new colony of Georgia in 1734 and founded Ebenezer on the Savannah. The dictionary records the Salzburg expulsion as the last mass religious expulsion in western Europe, and as the plainest instance of a confessing people kept by Scripture alone, with no minister, for two hundred years.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines emigration as the removal from one country to another; an edict as a public ordinance; a refugee as one who flees for safety; a colony as a body of settlers; and perseverance as continuance in a state of grace.

expand to see more

EMIGRATION, n. The act of removing from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.

EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order or ordinance by authority.

REFUGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country for safety.

COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.

PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any thing undertaken; in theology, continuance in a state of grace to a state of glory.

Key Scripture

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

Psa 119:54 — "Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage."

Mat 10:23 — "But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come."

Heb 11:16 — "But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city."

Modern Corruption

Austrian archbishopric whose 1731 edict expelled some twenty thousand Protestants from its Alpine valleys, many settling in East Prussia and in Georgia.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the expulsion of a population for its religion, carried out in 1731 by a Christian prelate against people who had committed no crime but possession of Lutheran books. Children under twelve were kept back. The dictionary names it as theft and kidnapping with an episcopal signature, and sets beside it the description Hebrews gives of such people, who die without receiving what was promised and are commended for it: they “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that a people may be kept by the word alone. These valleys had no pastors for generations and kept the faith by reading, by households and by memory, which is the psalmist's own account of how a man survives displacement: “Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psa 119:54). Christ licenses the flight itself, “But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23), and Hebrews names what the exiles were actually looking for, “a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16). Some of them found a river in Georgia and called the place Ebenezer, which is a stone of help.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parepidemos (G3927), a sojourner; Hebrew magur (H4033), a dwelling as a stranger; Greek patris (G3968), a country.

expand to see more

Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a resident foreigner, a pilgrim; “they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth”, Hebrews 11:13.

Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, a foreigner; “that they were strangers and pilgrims”, Hebrews 11:13.

Hebrew magur (H4033) — a sojourning, a dwelling as a stranger; “in the house of my pilgrimage”, Psalm 119:54.

Hebrew zimrah (H2172) — a song, music; “Thy statutes have been my songs”, Psalm 119:54.

Greek patris (G3968) — a fatherland, a country; “a better country, that is, an heavenly”, Hebrews 11:16.

Usage

"“they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) — the commendation of the expelled."

"“Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psa 119:54) — how valleys without pastors kept the faith."

"“a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16) — what the Salzburgers were actually looking for."
